title: Clostridioides difficile Infection
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is a significant cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis. It is a major healthcare-associated infection, particularly in low-resource settings where diagnostic tools may be limited. Understanding its transmission and clinical presentation is crucial for effective management.

sections.p: Clostridioides difficile (formerly Clostridium difficile) is an anaerobic, spore-forming bacterium that causes a spectrum of diseases ranging from asymptomatic colonization to severe, life-threatening pseudomembranous colitis. It is a common cause of healthcare-associated infections globally, exacerbated by antibiotic use which disrupts normal gut flora. In East African and other low-resource hospitals, the burden can be substantial, often complicated by delayed diagnosis and limited access to specific treatments.
b: CDI is a leading cause of hospital-acquired diarrhea.
Recent antibiotic use is the most significant risk factor.
Severity ranges from mild diarrhea to fulminant colitis.
Spore formation allows environmental persistence and transmission.

sections.p: Clostridioides difficile is a Gram-positive, obligate anaerobic, spore-forming bacillus. Its pathogenicity is primarily mediated by the production of two major toxins: Toxin A (an enterotoxin) and Toxin B (a cytotoxin). Some strains also produce a binary toxin, which is associated with more severe disease.
b: Gram-positive, rod-shaped bacterium.
Obligate anaerobe, meaning it thrives in oxygen-free environments.
Forms highly resistant spores, enabling survival outside the host.
Produces Toxin A and Toxin B, which damage intestinal epithelial cells.

sections.p: CDI is primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route, often through contaminated hands of healthcare workers or environmental surfaces. Spores are ingested, survive gastric acidity, and germinate in the colon, particularly when the normal gut microbiota is disrupted by antibiotics. The vegetative forms then multiply and produce toxins, leading to disease.
b: Fecal-oral transmission is the main route.
Spores are highly resistant to disinfectants and can persist in the environment.
Antibiotic use disrupts the normal gut flora, allowing C. difficile to proliferate.
Healthcare settings are common sites for transmission due to high patient turnover and antibiotic use.

sections.p: CDI manifests as diarrhea, which can range from mild and self-limiting to severe, leading to pseudomembranous colitis. Pseudomembranous colitis is characterized by the formation of yellowish-white plaques (pseudomembranes) on the colonic mucosa, composed of neutrophils, dead epithelial cells, and inflammatory debris. Complications include toxic megacolon, bowel perforation, and sepsis.
b: Diarrhea is the hallmark symptom, often watery and foul-smelling.
Abdominal pain, cramping, fever, and leukocytosis are common.
Pseudomembranous colitis is a severe form, visible on endoscopy.
Toxic megacolon and intestinal perforation are life-threatening complications.
Can be both nosocomial (hospital-acquired) and community-acquired.

sections.p: Diagnosis of CDI relies on clinical suspicion, especially in patients with recent antibiotic use and diarrhea, combined with laboratory confirmation. In low-resource settings, clinical assessment and basic stool microscopy might be the initial steps, followed by more specific tests if available. It is crucial to test only diarrheal stool, as asymptomatic colonization is common.

t.b: To look for inflammatory cells (e.g., neutrophils) and rule out other causes of diarrhea. Presence of many neutrophils suggests inflammation but is not specific for CDI. If specific tests are unavailable, this can support a diagnosis of inflammatory diarrhea.

t.a: Stool C. difficile Toxin A/B EIA (Enzyme Immunoassay)
t.b: To detect the presence of C. difficile toxins in stool. A positive result confirms active toxin production and disease. This is often the primary diagnostic test where available, but sensitivity can vary.

t.a: Stool C. difficile GDH (Glutamate Dehydrogenase) EIA
t.b: To screen for the presence of C. difficile antigen. A positive result indicates the presence of the organism but not necessarily toxin production. It is highly sensitive but not specific for active disease. Often used as a screening test in a two-step algorithm.

t.a: PCR for C. difficile toxin genes
t.b: To detect the genes encoding C. difficile toxins. This is highly sensitive and specific for toxigenic C. difficile. A positive result indicates the presence of a toxin-producing strain. This is the most accurate test but may not be available in all settings.

To visualize the colonic mucosa for pseudomembranes. This is typically reserved for severe cases or when diagnosis is unclear, especially if imaging suggests colitis. Direct visualization of pseudomembranes is diagnostic of pseudomembranous colitis.

To assess for complications like toxic megacolon or bowel perforation. Findings such as colonic dilation (over 6 cm) or free air under the diaphragm indicate severe disease requiring urgent intervention. This is often available even in low-resource settings.

sections.p: Management of CDI involves discontinuing the inciting antibiotic, initiating specific anti-CDI therapy, and providing supportive care. Infection control measures are paramount to prevent spread. In settings where specific anti-CDI drugs are limited, judicious antibiotic use and strict hygiene become even more critical.
b: Discontinue the offending antibiotic if possible.
First-line treatment for mild-moderate CDI is oral metronidazole.
For severe CDI, oral vancomycin is preferred; metronidazole is an alternative if vancomycin is unavailable.
Fidaxomicin is an alternative for recurrent or severe CDI, but often not available in low-resource settings.
Supportive care includes hydration and electrolyte replacement.
Strict infection control: hand hygiene (soap and water, not alcohol-based rubs, for spores), contact precautions, and environmental cleaning with sporicidal agents.
Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is an option for recurrent CDI, but highly specialized.

sections.p: Examiners will test your ability to integrate clinical presentation with diagnostic and management strategies, especially considering resource limitations. Focus on the 'why' behind each decision.
These topics are closely related to Clostridioides difficile infection and are important for a comprehensive understanding.

faq.q: Can C. difficile infection occur without prior antibiotic use?
faq.a: Yes, C. difficile can be community-acquired, though it is less common. Risk factors in these cases can include proton pump inhibitor use, older age, and contact with healthcare settings or infected individuals.

faq.q: Why is C. difficile so difficult to eradicate from the hospital environment?
faq.a: C. difficile forms highly resistant spores that can survive on surfaces for long periods and are not killed by many common hospital disinfectants or alcohol-based hand rubs, making environmental control challenging.

faq.q: What is the role of probiotics in preventing or treating C. difficile infection?
faq.a: The evidence for probiotics in preventing or treating C. difficile infection is mixed and not consistently strong enough to recommend routine use. Some studies suggest a potential benefit in prevention, but more research is needed.
